content: Leptospirosis is a disease with significant clinical and public health implications, caused by the globally distributed Leptospira bacteria. In populations exposed to the pathogen, the attack rate can range from 1 in 4 to 2 in 5 individuals, and in some cases, mortality rates have exceeded 10%. The role of antibiotic therapy in managing leptospirosis has been uncertain. To evaluate the risks and benefits of antibiotic therapy for leptospirosis, a systematic review was conducted. The search included databases such as the Cochrane Hepato-Biliary Group Controlled Trials Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, and the Science Citation Index Expanded, with no restrictions on language. The search was supplemented by manual methods and concluded in November 2011. Randomized clinical trials specifically assessing antibiotics for leptospirosis were included to evaluate benefits, while a broader range of studies was reviewed to assess potential harms. Data collection and analysis followed the Cochrane Handbook and the practices of the Cochrane Hepato-Biliary Group. Seven randomized trials were included in the review. Four trials, involving 403 patients, compared antibiotics to placebo or no intervention, while three trials compared different antibiotic regimens. All trials were found to have a high risk of bias, and the severity of leptospirosis varied among participants. The ability to pool data for meta-analysis was limited. In the four trials comparing antibiotics to placebo, mortality was reported, and parenteral penicillin was used in all cases. However, two of these trials reported no deaths. Among the remaining two trials, 16 out of 200 patients (8.0%) in the antibiotic group died, compared to 11 out of 203 patients (5.4%) in the placebo group. The fixed-effect odds ratio (OR) for mortality was 1.56 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.70 to 3.46), while the random-effects OR was 1.16 (95% CI 0.23 to 5.95). Heterogeneity for mortality outcomes was moderate (I² = 50%). Only one trial, involving 253 patients, reported the duration of hospitalization. It found no significant difference between the penicillin and placebo groups (8.9 days versus 8.8 days; mean difference [MD] 0.10 days, 95% CI -0.83 to 1.03). Two trials, involving 71 patients, reported the duration of clinical illness. Parenteral penicillin reduced the duration of illness to 4.7 to 5.6 days compared to 7.7 to 11.6 days in the placebo group. However, while the fixed-effect model showed a significant reduction (MD -2.13 days, 95% CI -2.46 to -1.80), statistical significance was lost under the random-effects model (MD -4.04 days, 95% CI -8.66 to 0.58). Heterogeneity for this outcome was high (I² = 81%). In a single trial of 79 patients, the duration of fever was assessed, and no significant difference was found between the antibiotic and placebo groups (6.9 days versus 6.6 days; MD 0.30 days, 95% CI -1.26 to 1.86). Two trials, involving 332 patients with relatively severe or late-stage leptospirosis, showed a trend toward increased dialysis in the penicillin group compared to placebo (25.8% versus 18.4%), but the effect was small and not statistically significant (OR 1.54, 95% CI 0.91 to 2.60). When comparing one antibiotic to another, no statistically significant differences were observed. For mortality, comparisons included cephalosporin versus penicillin (two trials: 3.4% versus 5.2%; fixed-effect OR 0.65, 95% CI 0.23 to 1.87, I² = 16%), doxycycline versus penicillin (one trial: 2.5% versus 4.5%; OR 0.54, 95% CI 0.10 to 3.02), and cephalosporin versus doxycycline (one trial: 1.1% versus 2.5%; OR 0.45, 95% CI 0.04 to 5.10). No adverse events related to therapy reached statistical significance. In conclusion, there is insufficient evidence to definitively recommend for or against the use of antibiotics in the treatment of leptospirosis. Among hospitalized survivors, antibiotics may reduce the duration of clinical illness by two to four days, but this finding was not statistically significant. The choice of antibiotic—whether penicillin, doxycycline, or cephalosporin—does not appear to affect mortality or the duration of fever. The benefit of antibiotic therapy, particularly in severe cases of leptospirosis, remains unclear. Further clinical research is needed, including trials that test a broader range of therapies against placebo.
